lesson.title: When Agreement Becomes the Enemy of Good Decisions
lesson.summary: A breakdown in group decision making, described by Irving Janis, in which the desire for harmony and consensus causes a cohesive group to suppress dissent and disregard realistic alternatives.
lesson.body:
Group polarization shows that discussion can push a group's opinions toward an extreme. Groupthink, a related but distinct concept developed by psychologist Irving Janis, describes what happens when a tightly knit, highly cohesive group becomes so committed to maintaining agreement and unity that it stops evaluating its options realistically. Janis coined the term after studying a series of American foreign policy failures, and argued that the very cohesiveness that makes a group feel effective can also make it dangerously bad at decision making.

Janis described a cluster of warning signs. Members may develop an illusion of invulnerability that encourages excessive risk taking. Dissent gets quietly discouraged, sometimes because individual members censor their own doubts rather than voice them, and sometimes because self-appointed mindguards actively shield the group from information that might disrupt consensus. The group may construct an illusion of unanimity, mistaking silence for agreement, and may stereotype outside critics as too weak or biased to take seriously.

Janis's central case study was the 1961 Bay of Pigs invasion, in which President Kennedy's advisors, a small, cohesive, high status group, approved a poorly vetted CIA plan to invade Cuba that failed badly and, in hindsight, had serious flaws that went largely unchallenged beforehand. Janis argued the group's cohesion and desire to preserve a sense of consensus discouraged the kind of hard questioning that might have caught the plan's problems in advance. Later analysts have applied the same framework to other disasters, including the 1986 Space Shuttle Challenger explosion, where engineers' warnings about a component failure were reportedly not pressed hard enough up the chain of a schedule driven organization.

It is worth being honest about the limits of groupthink as a scientific concept. Janis built the theory mainly from retrospective case studies of famous decisions that had already gone wrong, which is a useful way to generate an idea but a weaker way to test one, and later experimental and organizational research has found only mixed support for the claim that Janis's exact symptoms reliably predict bad group decisions. Even so, the concept remains widely used because it captures something real about cohesive groups, and it has produced practical countermeasures used in real organizations, such as deliberately assigning someone to play devil's advocate, inviting outside experts to challenge the group's assumptions, and collecting private, anonymous input before an open discussion locks people into a shared position.
